common_name: Silver Lining Climbing Hydrangea (White-Edged Variegated Climbing Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container vines in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade against a wall, fence, or sturdy tree trunk the vine can self-cling to.

directions: Silver Lining carries heart-shaped, gray-green leaves edged in an irregular band of creamy white, giving it a cooler, frostier look than the gold-margined 'Firefly' or 'Miranda'. It clings to brick, stone, or wood with aerial rootlets and needs no trellis, producing the same flattened white lacecap flower clusters in early to midsummer once established. Like all climbing hydrangea selections it grows slowly for the first few seasons while building a root system, then becomes a vigorous, long-lived climber. Site it out of hot afternoon sun, which can scorch the pale leaf margins, and prune only after flowering to control size.

common_name: Flying Saucer Climbing Hydrangea (Large-Flowered Climbing Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container vines in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade against a wall or tree trunk the vine can self-cling to with aerial rootlets.

directions: Flying Saucer is grown for flower size rather than foliage color, carrying plain glossy green, heart-shaped leaves and unusually large, flattened lacecap flower heads whose wide collar of creamy-white sterile florets dwarfs the typical species bloom. It self-clings to masonry and bark by aerial rootlets, so no support structure is needed once it has rooted in. As with other climbing hydrangea selections, expect little visible top growth for the first couple of seasons while the root and holdfast system develops, followed by steady, long-term climbing. Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich soil and prune lightly after flowering only to keep it within bounds.

common_name: Kuga Variegated Climbing Hydrangea (Dark-Leaved White-Mottled Climbing Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container vines in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade against a wall, fence, or tree the vine can self-cling to.

directions: Kuga Variegated stands apart from the brighter gold-edged selections by pairing dark, glossy green leaf centers with irregular white mottling scattered across the blade rather than confined to the margin, giving a subtler, almost hand-spattered variegation. Like the species it clings by aerial rootlets, flowers with flattened white lacecap heads in early summer on established wood, and develops exfoliating cinnamon bark with age. Variegated selections are generally slower and less vigorous than the plain green form, so expect an extended establishment period before significant climbing begins. Grow in cool, evenly moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, with protection from hot afternoon sun that can burn the white-mottled leaf tissue.

common_name: Early Light Climbing Hydrangea (Cream-Emerging Foliage Climbing Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container vines in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade against a wall or sturdy tree trunk the vine can self-cling to.

directions: Early Light's new leaves open an almost ghostly cream-white before gradually greening over the season, creating a shifting two-tone effect across the vine rather than a fixed margin pattern. The heavy variegation slows its growth noticeably compared with the species, so it stays more restrained and takes longer to cover a wall or trunk, which suits gardeners who want a climbing hydrangea for a smaller shaded space. It clings by aerial rootlets and produces the same mildly fragrant white lacecap flowers once mature. Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, shielding it from intense afternoon sun that can scorch the pale new growth, and be patient through its slow early years.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; Pixie stays compact and dense rather than sprawling like the species.

directions: A naturally occurring dwarf sport of the Fatsia-and-ivy hybrid, Pixie has leaves roughly half the size of the typical species and very short internodes, giving it a dense, twiggy, upright-bushy habit that stays noticeably smaller and tidier than other Fatshedera selections. It works well as a shrubby foundation plant, container specimen, or indoor plant where the sprawling habit of plain Fatshedera would be unwelcome. Grow it in filtered to full shade with humus-rich, well-drained soil, since it reverts to lax growth and scorches in strong direct sun. Little pruning is needed beyond removing any longer, atypical shoots to preserve its compact form.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Yvonne's Petticoat tolerates more light than most Fatshedera selections but still prefers shelter from hot sun.

directions: Discovered in the garden of Yvonne Pupatti of Marshallberg, North Carolina and introduced by Plant Delights Nursery in 2005, Yvonne's Petticoat forms a dense, bushy mass of woody stems clothed in solid green, star-shaped leaves with a wavy, ruffled edge but no variegation. Its sturdier, shrubbier habit holds up well as an unclipped foundation planting or informal hedge in shaded gardens, and it accepts more sun than most Fatshedera without scorching. Small rounded clusters of greenish-white flowers may appear on mature wood in fall. Grow in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and prune only to shape, since it needs little routine maintenance once established.

common_name: Barbara Ann Wood Vamp (Glossy-Leaved Native Climbing Hydrangea Vine)

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown vines in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in part to full shade; this selection is valued for extra-glossy foliage and strong self-clinging habit.

directions: Barbara Ann is a named selection of the southeastern native wood vamp chosen for its especially large, glossy, dark-green leaves and vigorous self-clinging growth up walls, fences, and tree trunks by aerial rootlets. Like the species, it bears clusters of small, sweetly fragrant white flowers in late spring, lacking the showy sterile bracts of Asian climbing hydrangeas but more fragrant and genuinely attractive to pollinators. It tolerates deeper shade than almost any other vigorous climbing vine and holds its foliage semi-evergreen to evergreen in milder zones. Keep the root zone consistently moist and mulched, reflecting its native habitat along streambanks and swampy forest edges, and avoid letting it dry out in its first two seasons while it establishes.

common_name: Vickie Wood Vamp (Native Climbing Hydrangea Vine Selection)

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown vines in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in part to full shade.

directions: Vickie is a selection of the native wood vamp singled out for superior vigor and a particularly heavy show of fragrant white flower clusters in late spring compared with typical wild plants. It climbs by clinging aerial rootlets without need of a trellis, scaling tree trunks, brick, or stone, and its glossy, semi-evergreen to evergreen foliage provides year-round cover of shaded surfaces in warmer zones. As one of the few vigorous self-clinging vines genuinely at home in deep shade, it suits naturalized woodland plantings, shaded walls, and streamside gardens. Keep soil consistently moist and acidic, mulch to protect the root zone, and expect a slow initial establishment period typical of climbing hydrangea relatives before active climbing accelerates.

common_name: Trehane Form Sausage Vine (Free-Flowering Evergreen Shade Vine)

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring against a sheltered fence, pergola, or trellis in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Trehane Form flowers more freely than typical seed-grown plants.

directions: Trehane Form is a selected clone of the Chinese sausage vine chosen for its rounded, glossy evergreen leaflets and notably heavier flowering than ordinary seedling plants. In spring it bears small, sweetly scented, bell-shaped flowers in cream-white male clusters and pinkish-purple female clusters on the same twining vine, occasionally followed by edible purple sausage-shaped fruit where both sexes are present. It twines around wires, trellises, or other vines rather than clinging by rootlets, so it needs something to wrap around from the start. Grow in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with shelter from harsh winter wind, since foliage can be damaged at the colder end of its range.
